title: Accidental extubation
banner: DRAFT, NOT clinically reviewed. Fictional scenario specification; never imported, published or shown to learners.
learning_objectives: Recognise suspected displacement or accidental extubation and call for help immediately.
Stay with the patient and support the airway until help arrives.
Leave reintubation and airway decisions to the clinicians responsible.
Report the event and review the contributing factors.

sources.use: patient-ventilator assessment CPG: securement, cuff and assessment statements
Indexed primary consensus recommendations on sustained exhaled CO2 and reconfirmation.
ISCCM 2024 weaning position statement: unplanned extubation and reintubation indications, selected recommendation text
PUMA 2026 tracheal extubation guidance: unplanned extubation and observation for deterioration, selected indexed text

required_sources: Unit procedure for emergency airway support, unplanned-extubation prevention and competency; full independent appraisal of the cited statements
gaps: No published clinical scenario may exist until the review phase: this is a specification only.
The branching content, consequences and scoring are the author's reading of the cited sources and have had no clinical review.
Selected ISCCM 2024 and PUMA 2026 recommendations now supplement recognition, deterioration and escalation; device-specific rescue maneuvers still require local instruction.
Reintubation warning signs are described at teaching level; indications in an individual patient, technique and rescue procedures remain clinician decisions.
permissions: Cited sources are paraphrased only; see the licensing register for each source's reproduction status.
setting: A fictional ventilated adult who was agitated overnight.

steps.info: During bedside care, an intubated adult becomes agitated. The tube marking has shifted outward from the documented depth, an audible leak develops and saturation begins to fall. Effective ventilation and tube position are uncertain.
steps.prompt: What is the immediate priority when displacement of an endotracheal tube is suspected?

options.text: Stay with the patient, call for help immediately and give oxygen and airway support per the unit's protocol.
options.feedback: Suspected displacement and accidental extubation call for immediate escalation, and the nurse stays with the patient. A displaced tube may no longer provide effective ventilation. Assess the patient's breathing and oxygenation, summon the airway team immediately and follow the emergency pathway; do not blindly advance the tube.
options.consequence: Immediate airway-team assistance and authorized support may limit the duration of inadequate ventilation.

options.text: Push the tube back in to where it was using the previously recorded depth, then reassess the leak and oxygen saturation.
options.feedback: Repositioning an airway device is not a safe nursing improvisation and may cause harm.
options.consequence: Blind advancement could worsen displacement or airway injury and delay effective rescue.

options.text: Leave the bedside to find a doctor and return with the airway team, rather than asking a colleague to activate emergency help.
options.feedback: Calling for help is right, but leaving the patient removes airway support at the worst moment.
options.consequence: Leaving the patient could delay airway support while oxygenation and ventilation deteriorate.

steps.info: At the next shared checkpoint the tube is out. The patient makes spontaneous respiratory efforts but is struggling, saturation is falling and chest movement is inadequate. The trained airway team is on its way.
steps.prompt: What must happen while the airway team is responding if spontaneous breathing is ineffective?

options.text: Stay with the patient, assess whether breathing is effective and activate the emergency airway response. Provide oxygen and trained ventilation assistance when indicated under the approved emergency pathway while colleagues prepare equipment. Do not wait for the airway team if ventilation is inadequate.
options.feedback: Oxygen delivery alone may not correct inadequate ventilation after accidental extubation. Prompt assessment and appropriate ventilation support within training and the local emergency pathway take priority while the responsible airway clinicians arrive. Report airway obstruction, inability to manage secretions, respiratory exhaustion, reduced consciousness or arrest immediately; these are indications for urgent trained-team assessment for reintubation in the ISCCM statement. An apparently acceptable saturation must not delay assessment or rescue if ventilation is failing.
options.consequence: Early trained ventilation support and ongoing monitoring may reduce the time without adequate ventilation.

options.text: Try to reintubate the patient yourself.
options.feedback: Reintubation is a skilled airway procedure for the responsible clinicians.
options.consequence: An untrained reintubation attempt could cause airway injury and delay effective support.

options.text: Switch off the monitor to reduce the alarms and concentrate.
options.feedback: Monitoring must continue during an airway emergency.
options.consequence: Switching off monitoring could conceal worsening oxygenation or circulation and impede the team's assessment.

steps.info: At the final shared checkpoint the airway team has reintubated the patient. Saturation has improved and waveform capnography is connected. The team needs to confirm sustained exhaled carbon dioxide, ongoing ventilation and securement; the incident still needs factual review.
steps.prompt: Which verification and follow-up best address immediate airway safety and recurrence risk?

observations.label: Tube position
observations.value: Position checked by airway team; waveform capnography connected

observations.label: Waveform capnography
observations.value: Connected; sustained exhaled carbon dioxide to be confirmed with team

options.text: Confirm with the airway team that placement and ongoing ventilation have been assessed, including sustained exhaled carbon dioxide on waveform capnography. Continue monitoring, give factual handover, report the incident and review agitation and securement.
options.feedback: Sustained exhaled carbon dioxide on waveform capnography is central to excluding oesophageal intubation. Reassess if the trace changes, the tube moves, or oxygenation deteriorates. An absent or lost reliable trace requires immediate airway-team assessment and emergency support; a depth mark or satisfactory saturation alone cannot confirm placement. Review contributing factors without blame. After stabilization, review documented tube position, securement and factors such as agitation or movement; prevention and monitoring are multidisciplinary.
options.consequence: Verification and a factual incident review may identify residual airway concerns and modifiable contributors to recurrence.

options.text: Say it was bound to happen and record nothing.
options.feedback: Incidents are recorded and reported so they can be learned from.
options.consequence: Failure to document could leave displacement risks and the sequence of rescue actions unrecognized.

options.text: Blame the night staff in the report.
options.feedback: A report states facts and actions, not blame.
options.consequence: Blame-focused reporting could discourage accurate reporting of contributing factors and prevent learning.

learning_points: Suspected displacement is an emergency: call for help and stay with the patient.
Assess effective breathing as well as oxygenation; provide trained emergency ventilation support if indicated under the local pathway while the airway team responds.
Report the event and review agitation, sedation and securement.
After reintubation, confirm the team's placement assessment and sustained waveform capnography; escalate loss of a reliable trace or renewed deterioration promptly.
Do not delay airway-team review for obstruction, exhaustion, secretion burden or reduced consciousness after unplanned extubation.
